newsitem.title: GERMANY: Kohl, Chirac quiet at start of informal talks.
newsitem.headline: Kohl, Chirac quiet at start of informal talks.

text.p: Chancellor Helmut Kohl and President Jacques Chirac met in Bonn on Wednesday evening for informal talks on Europe's single currency and reform plans amid growing signs of Franco-German differences.

Kohl said the meeting was "a completely normal visit" in a private atmosphere and would focus on "the European summit in June and all other questions". Chirac included the euro currency in his short list of topics for the talks.

"The conversation will be without a doubt serious and will also be without a doubt agreeable," he said. When a reporter shouted out a question on whether there were any problems between Bonn and Paris, he said with a smile: "No."
The two men then went into Kohl's official residence to dine on white asparagus with ham and new potatoes. French and German officials said there would be no statement afterwards.

Despite Chirac's assurances, officials and diplomats said there were still differences between the two partners over reforms the European Union wants to approve at its next summit in June in Amsterdam.
France has angered smaller EU members by pushing hard for a radical reduction in the number of European commissioners each member state can have.
Stressing the commission would become unwieldy if it expanded each time new members joined the EU, Paris proposed reducing the 20-member body to 10-12 rotating seats.
Consensus-minded Germany, aware of the stiff opposition to this from smaller EU members, leans towards a compromise that would allow almost all members to have a seat.
"The French proposal cannot be achieved for political reasons," said one foreign policy strategist in Kohl's Christian Democratic Union (CDU).

"The fact there are now so many proposals for rotation, junior commissioners without portfolio and so on, only shows we are still at the start of this debate," he said. "It will probably not be solved until the Amsterdam summit in June."
Linked to this issue is the question of the weighting of members' votes within the Council of Ministers to reflect the size of their respective populations.

Each enlargement of the EU undermines the dominant role the largest states -- Germany, France, Britain and Italy -- used to play by increasing the number of votes the smaller countries can amass against them.

Paris wants to reshuffle the number of votes each member has to ensure the bigger states cannot be easily outvoted. Bonn prefers a plan for a "double majority" by which a majority of member states and a majority of the EU population would be needed to approve policy decisions.
Although it seems like a case of squaring a circle, German officials insist Bonn and Paris will be able to come up with some sort of compromise in time for the Amsterdam summit.
Taking a longer view, the two countries' foreign ministries are considering ways to improve their own policy coordination to present a more united front in foreign affairs.
They have worked out proposals for closer consultation on the main issues, joint trips abroad by their foreign ministers and more personnel swaps between German and French ministries.
The suggestions are still at the planning stage and will not be on the agenda for Kohl and Chirac, a spokesman said.
German press commentators were not as optimistic as Bonn about the chances of effective reforms emerging in Amsterdam.

"The loudly proclaimed project of updating the Maastricht treaty is bogged down in crisis," Munich's Sueddeutsche Zeitung wrote on Wednesday. "Apart from calls to hang on, there is nothing that points to any success of these talks soon."
